tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five claims about pairs used in clinical and public-health writing, where familiar words carry narrower technical senses. Decide whether each account of the pair is accurate.
statements: In clinical usage "acute" and "severe" are interchangeable, so an infection recorded as "acute" is by definition more dangerous than one recorded as chronic.
Malaria described as "endemic" in a highland district is constantly present there at a predictable level, whereas an "epidemic" would mean cases climbing well above that expected baseline.
A ministry reporting the "incidence" of hepatitis C is counting everyone living with the infection, while "prevalence" would count only the new diagnoses recorded during the year.
"Quarantine" and "isolation" are two labels for a single measure, so a traveller with no symptoms and a patient with a confirmed infection are placed under the same order.
In a case report the rash an examining doctor observes is written up as a "symptom", while the headache the patient describes is recorded as a "sign".
tactical_explanations:
**A) In clinical usage "acute" and "severe" are interchangeable, so an infection recorded as "acute" is by definition more dangerous than one recorded as chronic.**

"Acute" is a statement about time course: it marks an illness that arrives quickly and runs a short course, whatever its intensity. "Severe" grades how bad the episode is, and the two scales move independently, which is why notes can record an acute mild sinusitis in one patient and a chronic severe one in the next. The sentence borrows danger from the severity scale and attaches it to the onset scale.

**Trap:** Everyday English uses "acute" to mean intense, and that habit is precisely what the clinical sense declines to follow.

Speed of onset and gravity are measured separately in a case note, so the claimed equivalence collapses and an acute infection remains the fast-arriving one rather than the automatically dangerous one.

**B) Malaria described as "endemic" in a highland district is constantly present there at a predictable level, whereas an "epidemic" would mean cases climbing well above that expected baseline.**

"Endemic" describes a disease that is permanently established in a population at a rate surveillance can anticipate, however high or low that rate happens to be. "Epidemic" is a comparative judgement against that anticipated rate, marking a rise steep enough to be abnormal for the place and season. The pair therefore works as baseline against departure from baseline, which is why an endemic district can still suffer an epidemic in a bad year.

Both terms are pinned to the same expected level and differ only in whether cases sit on it or shoot above it, so the description tracks how surveillance reports actually use them.

**C) A ministry reporting the "incidence" of hepatitis C is counting everyone living with the infection, while "prevalence" would count only the new diagnoses recorded during the year.**

"Incidence" counts fresh cases arising in a defined period and therefore measures how fast an infection is spreading. "Prevalence" counts everyone who has the condition at a given moment, whether they were diagnosed last week or a decade ago, and so measures the burden a health system is carrying. A long-lasting infection such as hepatitis C shows the gap plainly: prevalence stays high for years after incidence has been driven down by treatment.

The two counts have been swapped, so the sentence describes the burden measure as the flow measure and cannot stand as written.

**D) "Quarantine" and "isolation" are two labels for a single measure, so a traveller with no symptoms and a patient with a confirmed infection are placed under the same order.**

"Quarantine" separates people who may have been exposed but are not known to be infected, and it lasts as long as the incubation period requires. "Isolation" separates people who are known or strongly suspected to be infectious, and it lasts until they cease to be. The distinction decides who is monitored, for how long, and under what release criteria, which is why public-health law keeps the two orders apart.

Exposure and confirmed infection call for different periods and different release tests, so collapsing the two words also collapses a legal distinction that the traveller and the patient would each feel.

**E) In a case report the rash an examining doctor observes is written up as a "symptom", while the headache the patient describes is recorded as a "sign".**

A "symptom" is subjective: it is what the patient reports feeling, and nobody else can verify it directly. A "sign" is objective: it is what the clinician can see, hear, palpate or measure, and a second examiner should find it too. A visible rash is therefore the sign and the reported headache the symptom.

**Tip:** Ask who could confirm the finding without being told about it; if only the patient knows, it is a symptom.

The labels have been exchanged here, so the line fails — the rash is the sign and the headache the symptom.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line turns on a technical sense that everyday English has blurred: how fast an illness starts rather than how bad it is, a steady expected level rather than a departure from it, existing cases rather than new ones, exposure rather than confirmed infection, and what the patient feels rather than what the examiner can verify. Work out which axis the sentence is really measuring, then check that the word chosen belongs on that axis. Where a definition reads smoothly, test whether the two terms have quietly been handed each other's meanings.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Five statements about the near-synonyms used in ecology and conservation reporting. Judge whether each distinction is drawn correctly.
statements: "Habitat" names the place a species lives, while its "niche" is the role and range of conditions it occupies there, so two warbler species can share one stretch of woodland and still hold different niches.
"Invasive" is simply the technical label for "non-native", so a garden shrub brought in from another continent is classed as invasive in a conservation survey whether or not it spreads.

On the standard red lists "threatened" is the umbrella heading and "endangered" one of the categories beneath it, so every endangered amphibian counts as threatened while many threatened ones are not endangered.

"Drought" describes a climate that is permanently dry, while "aridity" describes a temporary shortfall against what a place normally receives, so the Atacama sits in perpetual drought while a rainforest can never be arid.
"Reuse" and "recycle" name the same stage of the waste hierarchy, so returning a glass bottle to be washed and refilled counts as recycling in the technical sense.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Habitat" names the place a species lives, while its "niche" is the role and range of conditions it occupies there, so two warbler species can share one stretch of woodland and still hold different niches.**

"Habitat" is an address: the physical setting, its vegetation and its structure. "Niche" is an occupation: the temperatures, food, nesting height and timing a species actually exploits, together with the part it plays in the wider system. Because the second is finer-grained than the first, birds feeding at different heights on different insects are partitioning niches inside a shared habitat.

Place and role are separate levels of description, and the woodland example sets each word at its own level, so the contrast is drawn exactly as ecologists draw it.

**B) "Invasive" is simply the technical label for "non-native", so a garden shrub brought in from another continent is classed as invasive in a conservation survey whether or not it spreads.**

"Non-native" is a statement of origin and nothing more: the species arrived through human agency rather than by its own range expansion. "Invasive" adds two further conditions, that the species establishes itself and spreads to the measurable detriment of native species or habitats. Most introduced garden plants never clear that bar, which is why surveys list far more non-natives than invasives.

Harm and spread are conditions the shorter label never claims, so the equation fails — the shrub is non-native, and only evidence of aggressive spread would make it invasive.

**C) On the standard red lists "threatened" is the umbrella heading and "endangered" one of the categories beneath it, so every endangered amphibian counts as threatened while many threatened ones are not endangered.**

"Threatened" is the grouping term covering the three ranked categories of elevated extinction risk. "Endangered" is the middle of those ranks, sitting above vulnerable and below critically endangered, and it carries specific criteria on population size, decline and range. That nesting is what makes the one-way relationship in the sentence hold: membership of the narrower rank guarantees membership of the wider group, never the reverse.

The sentence keeps the general heading above the specific rank and draws the implication in the direction that nesting allows, so it reads correctly.

**D) "Drought" describes a climate that is permanently dry, while "aridity" describes a temporary shortfall against what a place normally receives, so the Atacama sits in perpetual drought while a rainforest can never be arid.**

Aridity is the long-run property, built into a place's climate statistics and expected every year, which is why deserts are described as arid rather than as permanently drought-stricken. Drought is the deviation, defined against whatever that particular place normally receives, which makes it relative and temporary. A rainforest that misses a wet season is in drought while remaining far wetter than any desert, and the Atacama receiving its usual few millimetres is simply arid.

**Trap:** Both words mean dry in ordinary speech, which hides that one is a baseline and the other a departure from it.

The permanent condition and the temporary shortfall have been handed to the wrong words, so the line fails — the desert is arid, and it is the rainforest that can fall into drought.

**E) "Reuse" and "recycle" name the same stage of the waste hierarchy, so returning a glass bottle to be washed and refilled counts as recycling in the technical sense.**

"Reuse" keeps the object intact and puts it back into service in its existing form, which is why refill schemes and repair are ranked above recycling in waste policy. "Recycle" breaks the material down and reprocesses it into new feedstock, which recovers the substance but destroys the article and consumes energy doing so. A washed and refilled bottle has never been reprocessed at all.

**Tip:** If the object survives the process, the verb is reuse; if only the material survives, it is recycling.

The hierarchy separates these steps precisely because their environmental costs differ, so the refilled bottle belongs under reuse rather than recycling.
tasks.solution_overview: Conservation vocabulary is built from graded categories, so read each line for the extra condition one word imposes on the other: a role inside a place, harm on top of foreign origin, a rank inside a wider group, a deviation from a local norm, and reprocessing rather than continued service. Ask whether the narrower term could apply without its defining condition being met. Where a sentence flattens two terms into one, check what the policy or red list would lose by accepting that.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Five claims about pairs drawn from linguistics, teaching and folklore, each marking a different scope. Decide whether the contrast holds.
statements: "Accent" covers pronunciation alone, while "dialect" takes in vocabulary and grammar as well, so a speaker whose written prose is entirely standard may still have a strong regional accent.
"Syllabus" is the wider term for everything a school teaches across all its years, while "curriculum" lists the topics and readings of a single course.
A "formative" assessment is designed to feed back into teaching while the course is still running, whereas a "summative" one measures what has been learnt once it has ended.

"Empathy" means reconstructing another person's feelings from the inside, while "sympathy" means feeling for them from outside their situation, so a bereavement volunteer trained in empathy is being asked for more than sympathy.
In folklore scholarship a "legend" is the sacred narrative explaining how the world came to be, while a "myth" is set in remembered history and attached to named human figures.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Accent" covers pronunciation alone, while "dialect" takes in vocabulary and grammar as well, so a speaker whose written prose is entirely standard may still have a strong regional accent.**

"Accent" is confined to the sound system: vowels, consonants, rhythm and intonation. "Dialect" is the larger container, holding those sounds plus regional word choice and grammatical patterns such as distinctive past-tense forms. Because writing records words and grammar but not sound, a text can be free of dialect features while its author speaks with an unmistakable accent.

**Tip:** Anything that survives being written down belongs to dialect; what disappears on the page is accent.

The sentence keeps sound inside the smaller category and lets the larger one absorb grammar and lexis, which is exactly how linguists divide the two.

**B) "Syllabus" is the wider term for everything a school teaches across all its years, while "curriculum" lists the topics and readings of a single course.**

"Curriculum" is the broad programme of study: the whole set of subjects, aims and progression a school or degree offers. "Syllabus" is the narrower document attached to one course, setting out its topics, texts, sequence and assessment. Institutions therefore review a curriculum every few years and reissue syllabuses every term.

The sentence has put the small document in the large slot and the large programme in the small one, so the account is upside down — the curriculum is the whole, the syllabus one course within it.

**C) A "formative" assessment is designed to feed back into teaching while the course is still running, whereas a "summative" one measures what has been learnt once it has ended.**

"Formative" work is diagnostic and forward-looking: its purpose is to show teacher and student where the gaps are in time to close them, which is why it is often ungraded. "Summative" work looks back and certifies attainment against the stated outcomes, which is why it carries the marks that appear on a transcript. The same quiz can serve either function depending on when it falls and what is done with the result.

Purpose and timing are the two things that separate them, and the sentence names both correctly, so the distinction is sound.

**D) "Empathy" means reconstructing another person's feelings from the inside, while "sympathy" means feeling for them from outside their situation, so a bereavement volunteer trained in empathy is being asked for more than sympathy.**

"Sympathy" is a response directed at someone: concern, pity or fellow feeling offered from one's own standpoint. "Empathy" involves taking up the other person's standpoint and modelling the experience as they have it, which is a harder and more disciplined act. Training in listening skills targets the second precisely because the first comes unbidden.

Standpoint is the whole of the difference, and the sentence places the volunteer inside the other person's experience rather than beside it, so the comparison holds.

**E) In folklore scholarship a "legend" is the sacred narrative explaining how the world came to be, while a "myth" is set in remembered history and attached to named human figures.**

"Myth" is the term for narratives of origin set outside ordinary historical time and treated as sacred or foundational by the community that tells them. "Legend" covers stories set in a remembered past, populated by human figures who may have existed, and told as though they could in principle be true. The two labels answer different questions about a story: what kind of time it occupies and what claim to belief it makes.

The definitions have been switched, so the line does not hold — an origin narrative is the myth, and the tale of a named local hero is the legend.
tasks.solution_overview: Every pair here divides a large container from something inside it, or an inside standpoint from an outside one, so decide which member ought to be the broader term before reading on. Pronunciation sits inside dialect, one course sits inside a curriculum, and origin narratives sit in a different order of time from stories about remembered people. The two lines about teaching and about feeling reward a check on purpose: what the assessment is for, and whose standpoint the listener is adopting.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five statements about words that legal drafting keeps apart even though ordinary usage treats them as equivalent. Judge whether each account is accurate.
statements: A decision can be "lawful" and still be attacked as not "legitimate", because legitimacy concerns whether the way power was exercised is accepted as proper rather than whether it complied with the statute book.
"Allege" and "assert" are neutral equivalents, so a newspaper reporting that an inspector "alleges" the water samples were switched is presenting that account as established.

An "amnesty" lifts liability from a whole class of people at once, while a "pardon" releases one named individual, so a state can pardon a single protester without granting an amnesty to the movement.
"Liable" belongs to civil obligations to make good a loss while "guilty" belongs to criminal fault, so a teaching hospital can be liable for damages without anyone being found guilty of an offence.
A "statute" is passed by the legislature while a "regulation" is made under powers the statute delegates, so a regulation can be struck down for reaching further than the statute allowed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A decision can be "lawful" and still be attacked as not "legitimate", because legitimacy concerns whether the way power was exercised is accepted as proper rather than whether it complied with the statute book.**

"Lawful" is a technical verdict: the act falls within the powers the law confers and breaks no rule. "Legitimate" is a broader judgement about authority and acceptance, taking in whether the right body decided, whether those affected were heard, and whether the reasons given can be defended in public. The two come apart whenever a rule permits something that a community regards as an abuse of the power behind it.

Compliance and acceptance are answered by different tests, so a decision surviving the first can still fail the second, exactly as the sentence describes.

**B) "Allege" and "assert" are neutral equivalents, so a newspaper reporting that an inspector "alleges" the water samples were switched is presenting that account as established.**

"Assert" states a claim and leaves its status open, taking its colour from the surrounding text. "Allege" carries a built-in reservation: it marks the claim as made but not yet proved, which is why it belongs to pleadings, charge sheets and the careful reporting of accusations. That reservation is a legal safeguard rather than a stylistic flourish.

The verb is chosen precisely to withhold endorsement, so the sentence reads a signal of doubt as a signal of proof and cannot stand — reporting an allegation leaves the switching unproved.

**C) An "amnesty" lifts liability from a whole class of people at once, while a "pardon" releases one named individual, so a state can pardon a single protester without granting an amnesty to the movement.**

"Amnesty" operates by category, wiping away liability for a defined group and often for offences not yet prosecuted, which makes it a political instrument as much as a legal one. "Pardon" operates on an individual after conviction, relieving that person of the penalty while the conviction and the offence category remain untouched. Scope is therefore the dividing line, not mercy.

One act reaches a class and the other a person, and the sentence draws the consequence that follows from that difference in reach, so the description is accurate.

**D) "Liable" belongs to civil obligations to make good a loss while "guilty" belongs to criminal fault, so a teaching hospital can be liable for damages without anyone being found guilty of an offence.**

"Liable" answers a question about who must compensate, decided on the balance of probabilities and often without any wrongdoing by a named person, as when an employer answers for the acts of staff. "Guilty" answers a question about criminal responsibility, decided to a far higher standard and attaching to an individual defendant. Different courts, different standards, different consequences.

**Tip:** Ask what follows the finding. Money owed points to liability, punishment to guilt.

A damages award and a criminal conviction rest on separate tests, so the hospital can face the first without anyone facing the second, just as the sentence has it.

**E) A "statute" is passed by the legislature while a "regulation" is made under powers the statute delegates, so a regulation can be struck down for reaching further than the statute allowed.**

"Statute" is primary legislation, debated and enacted by the legislature itself. "Regulation" is made by a minister or agency exercising authority the statute has handed down, which is why it is quicker to produce and easier to amend. That delegated origin is also its weakness: a regulation lives inside the boundary of its parent statute and has no independent authority beyond it.

Delegated power is bounded power, so a court can indeed set aside a regulation for exceeding its statutory source, and the sentence traces that chain correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: These lines ask what a word commits its user to, so test each one against the machinery behind it: which body acted, which standard of proof applies, how many people are covered, and where the authority came from. Lawful and legitimate part company over acceptance rather than compliance, while liability and guilt part company over the standard and the consequence. One of the verbs of accusation is doing quiet work with the status of a claim, and reading it as neutral changes what the report is saying.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Five statements about the vocabulary of measurement and evidence in research writing. Decide whether each pair is described correctly.
statements: "Mass" measures how much matter an object contains while "weight" measures the gravitational force acting on it, so a sample crate keeps its mass aboard a lunar lander and loses most of its weight.

A "hypothesis" is a single testable proposition while a "theory" is an organised framework that has survived repeated testing, so one experiment can overturn a hypothesis without disturbing the theory that generated it.

A "specimen" is the individual physical item collected, while the "sample" is the set drawn to stand for a larger population, so a botanist can log two hundred specimens that together make up one sample.

"Weather" reports the state of the atmosphere over hours or days while "climate" reports the statistics of that weather across decades, so a single cold spring settles nothing about a warming climate.
A "census" attempts to count every member of a population while a "survey" questions a sample and generalises, so a national census carries no sampling error of the kind a survey has to report.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Mass" measures how much matter an object contains while "weight" measures the gravitational force acting on it, so a sample crate keeps its mass aboard a lunar lander and loses most of its weight.**

"Mass" is an intrinsic property expressed in kilograms and unchanged by where the object sits. "Weight" is a force, the product of that mass and the local gravitational field, and it is properly expressed in newtons. Ordinary speech uses the second word for both, which is harmless at the greengrocer and unusable in a spacecraft payload calculation.

**Tip:** If moving the object to the Moon changes the number, the quantity being reported is weight.

Only one of the two quantities depends on the local field, and the crate example puts the change on the right side of the pair, so the description works.

**B) A "hypothesis" is a single testable proposition while a "theory" is an organised framework that has survived repeated testing, so one experiment can overturn a hypothesis without disturbing the theory that generated it.**

A "hypothesis" is narrow and disposable by design: it states one expected relationship in terms specific enough to be contradicted by data. A "theory" in scientific usage is the opposite of a guess, being a structured explanation supported across many independent lines of evidence and capable of generating fresh hypotheses. Losing one prediction rarely touches the structure, though a long run of failures eventually will.

Scope and evidential weight both separate the two, and the sentence lets the smaller claim fall without pulling the larger one down with it, which is how the relationship actually works.

**C) A "specimen" is the individual physical item collected, while the "sample" is the set drawn to stand for a larger population, so a botanist can log two hundred specimens that together make up one sample.**

"Specimen" points at a thing you could hold: a pressed plant, a core, a vial of blood. "Sample" is a statistical notion, the subset selected from a population so that inferences can be drawn about the whole. One is counted in items, the other described by how it was drawn, which is why methods sections report sampling strategy rather than specimen strategy.

A physical unit and a selected set belong to different levels of description, and the herbarium example nests the first inside the second correctly, so the line is accurate.

**D) "Weather" reports the state of the atmosphere over hours or days while "climate" reports the statistics of that weather across decades, so a single cold spring settles nothing about a warming climate.**

"Weather" is the instantaneous condition: temperature, wind and precipitation at a place and time. "Climate" is the distribution those conditions form over a long reference period, conventionally thirty years, including its averages and its extremes. Because one is a draw and the other the shape of the distribution it was drawn from, no single draw can refute a claim about the shape.

A short record cannot speak to a long-run statistic, so the inference the sentence blocks is exactly the one the distinction is designed to block.

**E) A "census" attempts to count every member of a population while a "survey" questions a sample and generalises, so a national census carries no sampling error of the kind a survey has to report.**

A "census" aims at complete enumeration, which removes sampling error by definition though it leaves plenty of room for undercount, non-response and misreporting. A "survey" deliberately studies a fraction and uses probability theory to attach a margin of error to the estimates it produces. The choice between them trades cost and frequency against the kind of uncertainty a statistician must declare.

Enumerating everyone and estimating from a fraction produce different error structures, so the sentence is right that only one of the two owes its readers a sampling margin.
tasks.solution_overview: Research prose uses ordinary words as measuring instruments, so ask what each term is a measurement of before judging the pair. Two of these lines separate a property of the object from a property of its setting, and two separate one observation from the long-run pattern or population it belongs to. For the hypothesis and theory pair, weigh how much evidence each word claims to rest on, and notice that the smaller claim is meant to be expendable.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Five claims about pairs used in museums, conservation studios and literary criticism, where intent and scope do most of the work. Decide whether each description is accurate.
statements: In heritage practice "conserving" an object means returning it to the appearance it had when new, while "restoring" it means no more than halting further decay.
A "replica" is a copy made openly and acknowledged as a copy, while a "forgery" is a copy made to deceive, so intent rather than the quality of the workmanship separates the two.
A "memoir" must trace a whole life in sequence, whereas an "autobiography" is free to concentrate on a single episode or relationship.

A "parody" imitates a style in order to mock it, while a "pastiche" imitates without ridicule and often in homage, so a composer can write a pastiche of a baroque suite with no satirical intent at all.
A painting's "provenance" is the scholarly judgement about who painted it, while its "attribution" is the documented record of everyone who has owned it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In heritage practice "conserving" an object means returning it to the appearance it had when new, while "restoring" it means no more than halting further decay.**

Conservation is the minimal intervention: stabilise the material, control the environment, arrest deterioration and keep as much original fabric as possible. Restoration goes further and reconstructs losses so that the object reads as it once did, which necessarily involves judgement about a state nobody alive has seen. The professional preference for the first is precisely a preference for doing less.

**Trap:** Both words sound like repair, which hides the fact that only one of them adds material the object no longer has.

The two practices have been swapped, so the sentence fails — conserving is the arrest of decay and restoring the return to a former appearance.

**B) A "replica" is a copy made openly and acknowledged as a copy, while a "forgery" is a copy made to deceive, so intent rather than the quality of the workmanship separates the two.**

A replica declares itself: it may be superbly accurate, cast from the original mould and displayed beside a label saying so. A forgery may be technically inferior yet still be a forgery, because what defines it is the attempt to pass the object off as something it is not. Courts and catalogues therefore ask about purpose and presentation rather than about skill.

Deception is the defining ingredient, and the sentence locates the difference in intent rather than craftsmanship, which is exactly where museum practice locates it.

**C) A "memoir" must trace a whole life in sequence, whereas an "autobiography" is free to concentrate on a single episode or relationship.**

An autobiography undertakes the full arc, from origins onwards, and organises a life as a chronology. A memoir works from memory around a chosen theme, period or relationship, and it makes no promise of completeness; that narrower focus is what allows a writer to publish several. The word's root in memory rather than in life-writing is a useful reminder of the difference.

The obligations have been reversed, so the claim collapses — the whole-life chronology is the autobiography and the selective account the memoir.

**D) A "parody" imitates a style in order to mock it, while a "pastiche" imitates without ridicule and often in homage, so a composer can write a pastiche of a baroque suite with no satirical intent at all.**

Parody depends on exaggeration: it reproduces the mannerisms of a style so that the audience laughs at them, and it fails if the target is not recognised. Pastiche reproduces the same mannerisms in earnest, borrowing an idiom because it suits the material or honours a predecessor. The technique overlaps almost entirely; the attitude does not.

Attitude to the model is the whole distinction, and the sentence lets one imitate admiringly while the other imitates mockingly, so the contrast is correctly drawn.

**E) A painting's "provenance" is the scholarly judgement about who painted it, while its "attribution" is the documented record of everyone who has owned it.**

Provenance is the chain of custody: sales, inventories, bequests and export licences that trace an object from the studio to the present owner, and it is what a gallery consults when questions of looting or authenticity arise. Attribution is the connoisseurial and technical judgement assigning the work to a hand, a workshop or a follower, and it can change when new analysis appears. Strong provenance often supports an attribution, but the two answer different questions.

Ownership history and authorship judgement have been exchanged here, so the sentence does not hold — provenance follows the object, attribution names the artist.
tasks.solution_overview: Museum and literary vocabulary often separates two words by intent or by which question they answer rather than by any visible difference in the object, so ask what the practitioner is trying to achieve or record. Two of these lines look convincing until you notice that the definitions belong to the opposite terms, which a quick paraphrase of each word exposes. For the copying and imitation pairs, the decisive test is whether anyone is meant to be deceived or mocked.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five statements about verbs that grade how completely a problem has been dealt with. Judge whether each comparison matches careful technical usage.
statements: "Mitigate" and "eliminate" make the same claim about an outcome, so a scheme reported as mitigating flood risk in the valley has removed that risk.
A condition that merely "enables" an avalanche is correctly said to "trigger" it, since both verbs name the event that sets the slide in motion.
"Curb" claims only that something has been held in check, while "eradicate" claims it is gone for good, so a hospital campaign can curb the overuse of antibiotics for years without eradicating it.
"Inhibit" describes slowing or partly blocking a process while "prevent" claims it never occurs, so a compound that inhibits an enzyme in the dish need not prevent the disease in the patient.
"Alleviate" addresses how far a condition is felt while "cure" removes what is causing it, so a treatment can alleviate the pain of an incurable illness without altering its course.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Mitigate" and "eliminate" make the same claim about an outcome, so a scheme reported as mitigating flood risk in the valley has removed that risk.**

To mitigate is to make less severe: the hazard remains, but its likelihood or its consequences have been reduced to a level someone has judged tolerable. To eliminate is to take the hazard out of the system altogether so that no residual risk needs managing. Engineering reports keep the words apart because insurers, planners and residents draw very different conclusions from each.

**Tip:** Ask whether anything is left to monitor afterwards; mitigation always leaves a remainder.

A reduced hazard is not an absent one, so the inference fails — mitigating the flood risk leaves a smaller risk that still has to be lived with.

**B) A condition that merely "enables" an avalanche is correctly said to "trigger" it, since both verbs name the event that sets the slide in motion.**

To enable is to make something possible: a weak layer buried in the snowpack creates the conditions under which a slide can happen, sometimes for weeks before anything moves. To trigger is to supply the immediate cause at a particular moment, whether that is a skier, a cornice collapse or a gunshot. Avalanche forecasting depends on holding the two apart, because the enabling condition is what makes the slope dangerous and the trigger is only what finishes the job.

Background possibility and immediate cause sit at different points in the causal chain, so the sentence overstates the weaker verb — the buried layer enables the slide that something else triggers.

**C) "Curb" claims only that something has been held in check, while "eradicate" claims it is gone for good, so a hospital campaign can curb the overuse of antibiotics for years without eradicating it.**

Curb implies continuing pressure against a tendency that would otherwise return, which is why the verb suits behaviour and habits. Eradicate is absolute and, in public health, is reserved for the permanent removal of a pathogen or practice, with smallpox as the standard example of how rarely it is earned. A prescribing campaign restrains a habit rather than abolishing it.

Continuing restraint and permanent removal are different achievements, and the sentence claims only the modest one for the campaign, so it stands.

**D) "Inhibit" describes slowing or partly blocking a process while "prevent" claims it never occurs, so a compound that inhibits an enzyme in the dish need not prevent the disease in the patient.**

Inhibition is a matter of degree and is reported with a percentage or a concentration, since the process continues at a reduced rate. Prevention is binary and is claimed only where the outcome is stopped from arising at all. Laboratory results speak the language of inhibition precisely because the step from partial blockade to clinical benefit has still to be demonstrated.

A graded effect on a molecule does not license an absolute claim about an illness, and the sentence marks that gap rather than crossing it, so it is accurate.

**E) "Alleviate" addresses how far a condition is felt while "cure" removes what is causing it, so a treatment can alleviate the pain of an incurable illness without altering its course.**

Alleviate works on the burden: it lightens symptoms, distress or pressure without any claim about the underlying mechanism. Cure works on the cause and asserts that the condition itself has been ended. Whole branches of medicine exist because the first is achievable in many cases where the second is not.

Symptom and cause are separate targets, and the sentence keeps the treatment aimed at the first while conceding the second remains out of reach, which is how the pair is used.
tasks.solution_overview: Each verb here quietly grades how complete an intervention is, so read for the residue: what is left over once the action has been taken. Reduction, restraint and partial blockade all leave something behind, while removal, prevention and cure claim there is nothing left to manage. One line concerns causation rather than degree, and it repays asking whether the condition named makes an event possible or actually sets it off.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Five statements about the verbs and nouns academic writing uses to grade evidence and assign responsibility for a claim. Decide whether each is accurate.
statements: A writer "implies" and a reader "infers", so a discussion section can imply that the funder shaped the design while it is the reviewer who infers it.
"Indicate" reports that evidence points somewhere while "establish" claims the question is settled, so a single fossil can indicate an earlier migration without establishing one.
"Plausible" says an account hangs together well enough to be entertained while "probable" says it is more likely than not, so a plausible reconstruction of the fire can still be an improbable one.
"Rebut" means to disprove a claim conclusively, while "refute" means only to offer a counter-argument against it.
A "quotation" reproduces an author's wording while a "citation" points the reader to the source, so a review article can cite four hundred studies and quote almost none of them.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A writer "implies" and a reader "infers", so a discussion section can imply that the funder shaped the design while it is the reviewer who infers it.**

Implying is something a text or speaker does: meaning is put into circulation without being stated outright. Inferring is something the audience does: a conclusion is drawn from what was said, from what was left out, and from what the reader already knows. The verbs face in opposite directions along the same channel, which is why one takes the author as subject and the other the recipient.

**Tip:** Ask who is doing the work. Sending the hint is implying, picking it up is inferring.

Each verb is attached to the party that performs it here, so the division of labour the sentence describes is the standard one.

**B) "Indicate" reports that evidence points somewhere while "establish" claims the question is settled, so a single fossil can indicate an earlier migration without establishing one.**

Indicate is deliberately weak: it acknowledges that the data lean towards a conclusion while leaving room for other explanations. Establish is strong and effectively closes the question, which is why reviewers challenge it when the evidence is thin. A lone specimen is exposed to reworking, misdating and misidentification, so it can only point.

Evidential strength is what separates the two verbs, and the sentence gives the isolated find the weaker one, which is the honest description of what a single fossil can do.

**C) "Plausible" says an account hangs together well enough to be entertained while "probable" says it is more likely than not, so a plausible reconstruction of the fire can still be an improbable one.**

Plausibility is about internal coherence: the story is consistent with known physics, with the timeline and with the damage, so it deserves consideration. Probability is a comparative judgement against rival explanations, and an account can be perfectly coherent yet require a chain of coincidences that a simpler account does not. Investigators separate the two so that a neat narrative is not mistaken for a likely one.

Coherence and likelihood are assessed against different things, so the sentence is right that a well-constructed reconstruction may still lose the comparison with its rivals.

**D) "Rebut" means to disprove a claim conclusively, while "refute" means only to offer a counter-argument against it.**

In careful usage refute is the strong verb: it asserts that a claim has been shown to be false, and it should be used only where the demonstration has actually been made. Rebut is the weaker procedural verb, describing the act of arguing against a claim or answering it in reply, whether or not the answer succeeds. Legal pleadings and journal correspondence both rely on that asymmetry.

The strengths have been traded, so the line does not hold — refuting is the conclusive act, while rebutting is merely mounting the reply.

**E) A "quotation" reproduces an author's wording while a "citation" points the reader to the source, so a review article can cite four hundred studies and quote almost none of them.**

A quotation carries the original words across into the new text and takes quotation marks or an indented block. A citation is a pointer, giving enough bibliographic detail for a reader to find the work, and it accompanies paraphrase, summary and data reuse just as readily as it accompanies quoted words. Bibliometrics counts the pointers, not the borrowed sentences.

Reproducing words and directing a reader elsewhere are different services to the reader, so the review article the sentence imagines is behaving exactly as reviews normally do.
tasks.solution_overview: Academic prose grades its claims with small verbs, so weigh how much each one promises before accepting the comparison. Two of these lines separate a tentative signal from a settled conclusion, and one separates coherence from likelihood, which is a distinction that survives even when a story sounds convincing. The remaining lines turn on who performs the act or what the reference actually delivers, so identify the agent and the service in each case.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Five statements about engineering and computing terms whose everyday senses pull against their technical ones. Judge whether each account matches professional usage.
statements: "Robust" and "resilient" both grade how quickly a system recovers once it has failed, which is why engineers use the two words interchangeably in reliability reports.
"Encoding" a file makes it unreadable without a key, which is why security teams treat encoding and encryption as the same safeguard.

"Verification" asks whether a system was built to its specification while "validation" asks whether that specification met the real need, so software can pass verification and still solve the wrong problem.
In engineering "redundancy" names the wasteful duplication a good design removes, exactly as the word does when a public body announces redundancies among its staff.
A "heuristic" guarantees the best available answer while an "algorithm" offers only a rule of thumb that usually works.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Robust" and "resilient" both grade how quickly a system recovers once it has failed, which is why engineers use the two words interchangeably in reliability reports.**

Robustness is resistance: the system absorbs disturbance and carries on performing without entering a failed state at all. Resilience is recovery: the system may degrade or fail, but it returns to service quickly and with acceptable loss. Design choices differ accordingly, since one buys margin and hardening while the other buys redundancy, monitoring and fast restoration.

Only the second word is about what happens after failure, so the definition offered covers half the pair — a robust structure resists the shock that a resilient one recovers from.

**B) "Encoding" a file makes it unreadable without a key, which is why security teams treat encoding and encryption as the same safeguard.**

Encoding converts data into another representation for transport or compatibility, and the transformation is public and reversible by anyone who knows the scheme; base64 and character sets are the everyday examples. Encryption transforms data using a secret key so that recovery is infeasible without it, which is what makes it a security control rather than a formatting convenience. Confusing the two produces breach reports in which data described as protected was merely reformatted.

No secret is involved in the first process, so the claim collapses — encoding rearranges data for handling while only encryption withholds it from a reader.

**C) "Verification" asks whether a system was built to its specification while "validation" asks whether that specification met the real need, so software can pass verification and still solve the wrong problem.**

Verification is an internal check: tests, reviews and proofs establish that the artefact conforms to the requirements as written. Validation is an external check against the world, asking whether those requirements captured what users actually needed. The two are separated in safety standards because a faultless implementation of a misunderstood requirement is a familiar and expensive failure.

Conformance and fitness for purpose are assessed against different references, and the sentence draws precisely the consequence that separation is meant to warn about.

**D) In engineering "redundancy" names the wasteful duplication a good design removes, exactly as the word does when a public body announces redundancies among its staff.**

In reliability engineering redundancy is deliberate spare capacity: a second pump, a third sensor, an alternative power feed, provided so that one failure does not take the system down. Far from being removed, it is specified, costed and tested, and its absence is a finding against a design. The employment sense, in which a post is surplus and cut, is a separate development of the same root.

The technical sense values the duplication that the everyday sense condemns, so the equation fails — engineered redundancy is designed in on purpose.

**E) A "heuristic" guarantees the best available answer while an "algorithm" offers only a rule of thumb that usually works.**

An algorithm is a defined procedure with a guaranteed outcome for its stated problem, and in optimisation an exact algorithm returns the optimum or reports that none exists. A heuristic trades that guarantee for speed, producing a good answer quickly with no promise of optimality, which is why route planners and scheduling tools lean on them. The absence of a guarantee is the point of the word.

Guarantee and rule of thumb have been assigned to the wrong terms, so the line fails — the algorithm carries the promise and the heuristic supplies the shortcut.
tasks.solution_overview: Technical fields borrow ordinary words and then narrow them, so test each line against what an engineer would actually specify or measure. Two of these pairs are separated by whether the system resists a disturbance or recovers from one, and by whether a secret is involved at all; one turns on a word whose professional sense is the opposite of its workplace sense. Where a definition sounds sensible, check whether the guarantee it describes belongs to the other member of the pair.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five statements about words used in constitutional argument and public order, where scope and permanence carry legal weight. Decide whether each distinction is accurate.
statements: "Autonomy" is self-government exercised within another state's sovereignty while "independence" ends that relationship, so an autonomous region can run its own schools and courts and still hold no seat of its own at the United Nations.

"Sedition" covers speech or conduct urging resistance to lawful authority while "treason" requires a betrayal of the state itself, typically by aiding an enemy, so the pamphleteer and the spy answer different charges.

"Riot" is a legal classification requiring violence by an assembled group, while "protest" carries no such element, so applying the first word to a peaceful march alters the legal exposure of those on it and not merely the tone of the report.

A "moratorium" suspends an activity for a stated period with resumption still possible, while a "ban" is framed as permanent, so a moratorium on deep-sea mining is a lighter commitment than an outright prohibition.

"Sovereignty" is the ultimate authority a state claims over its territory while "jurisdiction" is the reach of a particular court or agency, so a tribunal may lack jurisdiction over a dispute arising in territory whose sovereignty nobody questions.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Autonomy" is self-government exercised within another state's sovereignty while "independence" ends that relationship, so an autonomous region can run its own schools and courts and still hold no seat of its own at the United Nations.**

Autonomy is delegated or entrenched self-rule over listed matters, with the outer shell of statehood, defence and foreign relations retained elsewhere. Independence transfers that shell as well, producing a state that recognises no superior authority and can join international bodies in its own name. Degree of self-rule therefore rises continuously while the change from one word to the other is a change in kind.

Internal self-rule and full statehood are different in kind rather than in amount, and the example keeps the region on the near side of that line, so the sentence works.

**B) "Sedition" covers speech or conduct urging resistance to lawful authority while "treason" requires a betrayal of the state itself, typically by aiding an enemy, so the pamphleteer and the spy answer different charges.**

Sedition is directed at the loyalty of others: it stirs up disaffection or resistance, and historically it has been prosecuted through words and publications. Treason is the graver offence, requiring an act against the state's existence or security, classically levying war against it or assisting a hostile power. The difference shows in the penalties and in the evidence each charge demands.

Inciting others and betraying the state are separate acts with separate proofs, so the sentence sorts the two figures correctly between the charges.

**C) "Riot" is a legal classification requiring violence by an assembled group, while "protest" carries no such element, so applying the first word to a peaceful march alters the legal exposure of those on it and not merely the tone of the report.**

Protest describes the purpose of a gathering and says nothing about its conduct. Riot is a defined public-order offence built on a threshold of unlawful violence by a number of people acting together, and the label brings powers of dispersal, arrest and heavier sentencing with it. Because the classification carries those consequences, using it loosely is not a stylistic choice.

One word describes an aim and the other triggers a legal test, so the sentence is right that swapping them changes far more than the temperature of the coverage.

**D) A "moratorium" suspends an activity for a stated period with resumption still possible, while a "ban" is framed as permanent, so a moratorium on deep-sea mining is a lighter commitment than an outright prohibition.**

A moratorium is a pause, usually justified by uncertainty and often tied to a review date or to evidence being gathered; it leaves the underlying activity lawful in principle. A ban removes that permission and is intended to hold until it is repealed. Negotiators reach for the first when agreement on the second is out of reach, which is why the choice of word is itself a political signal.

A timed suspension asks less of the parties than a prohibition, and the sentence grades the two commitments in that order, so it stands.

**E) "Sovereignty" is the ultimate authority a state claims over its territory while "jurisdiction" is the reach of a particular court or agency, so a tribunal may lack jurisdiction over a dispute arising in territory whose sovereignty nobody questions.**

Sovereignty is a claim about supreme authority and is answered at the level of states. Jurisdiction is a much narrower and highly technical question about whether a given body may hear a given matter, decided by subject, by parties, by time limits and by consent. A court routinely declines cases arising in its own state because one of those conditions has not been met.

**Tip:** Sovereignty is about who rules; jurisdiction is about which body may decide this particular case.

Authority over territory and competence over a case are answered by different tests, so the situation the sentence describes is entirely ordinary.
tasks.solution_overview: Constitutional vocabulary is graded by scope and by permanence, so ask how far each word reaches and how long it is meant to last. Self-rule inside a state and statehood itself differ in kind, a pause differs from a prohibition, and ultimate authority over land differs from a court's competence over one case. Two lines involve labels that carry legal consequences, so check whether the word merely describes conduct or actually triggers a test.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five statements about words that mark the register of a document or the agency behind an event. Judge whether each account of the pair is accurate.
statements: "Peruse" is the formal word for glancing quickly over a document, so a reviewer who perused the appendix spent very little time on it.
"Dwelling" is the administrative term for a unit of accommodation, so a housing census counts dwellings while a charity's fundraising letter speaks of homes.
"Ascertain" is a formal way of saying "estimate", so an investigator who has ascertained the cause of the warehouse fire is offering an approximation.
In a lender's records an account described as "in arrears" has by that fact been placed "in default", since the two terms mark the same point in a credit agreement.

"Expire" happens when a fixed term simply runs out, while "terminate" is an act someone performs, so a discharge permit expires on its own date but is terminated only when the regulator ends it early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Peruse" is the formal word for glancing quickly over a document, so a reviewer who perused the appendix spent very little time on it.**

In its established sense peruse means to read closely and in detail, which is why it appears in phrases such as perusing the accounts before a meeting. The verb for a quick pass is skim or scan, and the two describe opposite depths of attention. The mistaken sense is common enough to appear in job adverts, but careful editors still treat it as an error.

**Trap:** The formal ring of the word tempts readers to assume it means something loftier than plain reading, when it actually means more of it.

Close attention rather than a rapid glance is what the verb reports, so the conclusion fails — a reviewer who perused the appendix went through it thoroughly.

**B) "Dwelling" is the administrative term for a unit of accommodation, so a housing census counts dwellings while a charity's fundraising letter speaks of homes.**

Dwelling is defined for statistical purposes as a self-contained set of rooms intended for occupation, which lets an agency count structures consistently whether or not anyone lives in them. Home carries the emotional freight of belonging and cannot be counted, since one family can have a home in a caravan and another can own a dwelling it has never slept in. Each word suits the document that uses it.

Countable units and felt attachment are different things to write about, so the split between the statistical return and the appeal letter is exactly the split the two words maintain.

**C) "Ascertain" is a formal way of saying "estimate", so an investigator who has ascertained the cause of the warehouse fire is offering an approximation.**

Ascertain means to establish something as certain, usually by inquiry: the fact has been pinned down and can be reported without hedging. Estimate does the opposite work, offering an approximate value while acknowledging that the true one is unknown. Fire investigators use the first only when the evidence supports a definite finding, and reach for probable cause when it does not.

Certainty and approximation are opposite commitments, so the sentence reverses the force of the verb — an ascertained cause is one the investigator says has been settled.

**D) In a lender's records an account described as "in arrears" has by that fact been placed "in default", since the two terms mark the same point in a credit agreement.**

Arrears simply means that scheduled payments have been missed and an overdue balance has built up; a borrower one payment behind is in arrears and may clear it next month. Default is a contractual status triggered when the agreement's own conditions are met, commonly after a set period or a formal notice, and it unlocks remedies such as acceleration of the whole balance or enforcement. Lenders keep the terms distinct because the second changes what they are entitled to do.

A missed payment and a triggered contractual status are different stages, so the equation fails — arrears can accumulate for some time before the agreement treats the account as in default.

**E) "Expire" happens when a fixed term simply runs out, while "terminate" is an act someone performs, so a discharge permit expires on its own date but is terminated only when the regulator ends it early.**

Expire is intransitive and agentless: nobody does it, the calendar simply arrives at the end date written into the instrument. Terminate takes an agent and a decision, and it usually requires grounds, notice and a right of appeal. The distinction matters in regulation because an expired permit lapses quietly while a terminated one is an enforcement event with consequences on the record.

A date arriving and an authority acting are different causes of the same outcome, and the sentence assigns each verb to its own cause, so the description holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Formality is not the only thing a heavier word signals, so ask what each one commits its writer to: how much attention was paid, how certain a finding is, or who performed the act. Two lines here assume that a formal-sounding verb must mean something vaguer or quicker than its plain partner, when in fact it claims more. The remaining lines reward asking whether an event happened by itself or was brought about, and whether a stage in a process has really been reached.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five statements about terms that quantitative writing uses precisely and everyday speech uses loosely. Decide whether each distinction is drawn correctly.
statements: "Exponential" is an emphatic way of saying "rapid", so any steeply rising curve of measles cases can properly be described as exponential.

An earthquake's "magnitude" measures the energy released and is a single figure for the event, while its "intensity" measures the shaking experienced at a given place, so one quake has one magnitude but many intensities.
"Accuracy" says how close readings sit to the true value while "precision" says how close they sit to one another, so a badly calibrated balance can be precise to the milligram and still be wrong.

In a results section "significant" reports that an effect is unlikely to be an accident of sampling while "substantial" claims that it is large, so a significant difference in reaction times may amount to a few milliseconds.
"Mean" and "median" name the same central value, so a sharply skewed distribution of examination marks yields the same figure whichever is reported.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Exponential" is an emphatic way of saying "rapid", so any steeply rising curve of measles cases can properly be described as exponential.**

Exponential growth has a specific shape: each increment is proportional to the current total, so the quantity doubles over a constant interval however large it becomes. A curve can climb steeply and yet be linear, or be slowing towards a ceiling, and outbreak curves usually bend once susceptible contacts run short. Epidemiologists therefore test for a constant doubling time before using the word.

**Tip:** Ask whether the doubling time stays the same; steepness alone never settles the question.

Steepness and proportional growth are different properties, so the word cannot be applied on the strength of a dramatic slope — many sharply rising outbreaks are not exponential at all.

**B) An earthquake's "magnitude" measures the energy released and is a single figure for the event, while its "intensity" measures the shaking experienced at a given place, so one quake has one magnitude but many intensities.**

Magnitude is derived from the seismic waves themselves and characterises the source, which is why a single number is quoted worldwide. Intensity is assessed from effects on people, buildings and ground at each location, so it falls away with distance and varies with soil and construction. That is how a moderate event on soft sediment can produce higher intensities than a larger one on rock.

One figure for the source and many for the places affected is exactly how seismic reporting is organised, so the sentence describes the pair correctly.

**C) "Accuracy" says how close readings sit to the true value while "precision" says how close they sit to one another, so a badly calibrated balance can be precise to the milligram and still be wrong.**

Accuracy is a comparison against a reference or accepted value and is degraded by systematic offsets. Precision describes the spread of repeated measurements and is degraded by random scatter, which is why it can be improved by better technique while the calibration error remains untouched. An instrument reading consistently five milligrams high is the standard illustration.

Closeness to truth and closeness to each other are independent, so a tightly repeatable but miscalibrated balance is a real possibility rather than a contradiction, and the sentence names it correctly.

**D) In a results section "significant" reports that an effect is unlikely to be an accident of sampling while "substantial" claims that it is large, so a significant difference in reaction times may amount to a few milliseconds.**

Statistical significance is a statement about compatibility with chance, and it depends heavily on sample size: with enough participants, a tiny difference clears the threshold. Substantial, important and meaningful are claims about magnitude and are argued with effect sizes and practical consequences. Journals ask for both because the first alone tells a reader nothing about whether the finding matters.

Detectability and size answer separate questions, and the sentence keeps the technical sense clear of the everyday one, so the account is right.

**E) "Mean" and "median" name the same central value, so a sharply skewed distribution of examination marks yields the same figure whichever is reported.**

The mean adds every value and divides by the count, so a handful of extreme marks pulls it towards the tail. The median takes the middle observation once the marks are ordered and is barely moved by those extremes. On a symmetric distribution the two coincide, which is exactly why the skewed case in the sentence is the one that separates them.

Skew is the condition under which the two measures diverge, so the claim fails — a long tail of very low marks drags the mean below the median while the middle mark stays put.
tasks.solution_overview: Quantitative vocabulary describes a shape, a source or a spread, so ask what each term is actually computed from before accepting the comparison. Two of these lines separate a property of the event from a property of the place or the reading, and one separates whether an effect is detectable from whether it is large. Where a word has drifted into everyday use as a general intensifier, check whether the technical condition behind it is being met.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five statements about clinical near-synonyms that separate laboratory conditions from ordinary practice, and partial improvement from resolution. Judge whether each is accurate.
statements: "Efficacy" reports how a treatment performs under trial conditions while "effectiveness" reports how it performs in ordinary practice, so a vaccine with high efficacy can show lower effectiveness once storage failures and missed appointments are in play.
"Remission" says a disease is undetectable for the moment while "recovery" claims a return to health, so a patient can be in remission and still be counted among those who have not recovered.
Every "contagious" disease is "infectious", though not every infectious one is contagious, since tetanus is acquired from the environment rather than from another person.
An "analgesic" removes sensation and awareness altogether, while an "anaesthetic" merely dulls pain that the patient can still feel.

A "screening" test is offered to people without symptoms in order to decide who needs further investigation, while a "diagnostic" test answers the question for one patient, so a positive screen is not yet a diagnosis.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Efficacy" reports how a treatment performs under trial conditions while "effectiveness" reports how it performs in ordinary practice, so a vaccine with high efficacy can show lower effectiveness once storage failures and missed appointments are in play.**

Efficacy is measured in a controlled setting with selected participants, monitored adherence and standardised handling, which is designed to isolate the treatment's own contribution. Effectiveness is measured in the population as it is, complete with cold chains that break, doses given late and people who never return for the second appointment. The gap between the two numbers is a health-system finding rather than a failure of the trial.

**Tip:** Efficacy answers whether it can work, effectiveness whether it does work where it is used.

Controlled conditions and everyday conditions are measured separately for good reason, so the drop the sentence describes is the expected pattern rather than a contradiction.

**B) "Remission" says a disease is undetectable for the moment while "recovery" claims a return to health, so a patient can be in remission and still be counted among those who have not recovered.**

Remission is a statement about current disease activity: signs and symptoms have receded, and in some conditions no cells or lesions can be found, but the possibility of relapse is built into the word. Recovery is a broader judgement covering function, strength and the resumption of ordinary life, which often lags months behind the disappearance of the disease. Oncology and rheumatology both need the narrower word for exactly that reason.

Absent disease activity and restored health are separate milestones, so the sentence is right that reaching the first leaves the second still to come.

**C) Every "contagious" disease is "infectious", though not every infectious one is contagious, since tetanus is acquired from the environment rather than from another person.**

Infectious is the wider term, covering any illness caused by a pathogen entering the body, whatever the route. Contagious narrows that to transmission between hosts, whether by direct contact, droplets or contaminated hands. Tetanus, legionellosis and many fungal infections are caught from soil, water or air without any infected person being involved, which places them inside the wider circle and outside the narrower one.

The nesting runs in one direction only, and the sentence states it in that direction with an example that sits precisely in the gap, so it holds.

**D) An "analgesic" removes sensation and awareness altogether, while an "anaesthetic" merely dulls pain that the patient can still feel.**

An analgesic relieves pain while leaving other sensation and consciousness intact, which is why a patient on one can still feel pressure and movement. An anaesthetic abolishes sensation in a region, or consciousness entirely, and is the reason surgery is tolerable at all. The functions have been handed to the wrong words.

**Trap:** Both words come from the vocabulary of pain relief, which makes the swap easy to read past.

The definitions belong to the opposite terms, so the line does not stand — the analgesic dulls pain while the anaesthetic removes sensation.

**E) A "screening" test is offered to people without symptoms in order to decide who needs further investigation, while a "diagnostic" test answers the question for one patient, so a positive screen is not yet a diagnosis.**

Screening is a population activity, tuned to miss as few cases as possible and therefore accepting a high number of false alarms. Diagnostic testing is tuned for confirmation in someone already suspected of having the condition, and it carries the accuracy needed to justify treatment. The two are designed with different trade-offs, which is why a screening programme always has a follow-up pathway attached.

Sorting a population and confirming one case are different jobs, so the caution the sentence attaches to a positive screen follows directly from how the test was designed.
tasks.solution_overview: Clinical vocabulary separates ideal conditions from messy ones and partial improvement from full resolution, so ask what each word is measured under and how much it claims. Two lines nest a narrow term inside a wider one, and the direction of that nesting is what makes the inference work or fail. One pair has simply been handed each other's definitions, which becomes obvious once you ask what a patient would still be able to feel.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five statements about pairs that look like restatements of one another but describe different stages, bases or standards. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Weathering" breaks rock down where it stands while "erosion" carries the loosened material away, so a sandstone facade can be deeply weathered without a grain of it having been eroded from the site.
A retailer's "markup" is calculated on what the goods cost while its "margin" is calculated on what they sell for, so the same twenty pounds of difference represents a larger markup than margin.

A "projection" states what follows if a stated scenario holds while a "prediction" asserts what will actually happen, so a modelling group can publish several projections without contradicting itself.

"Calibrating" an instrument adjusts its readings against a known standard while "validating" a model asks whether its outputs match independent observations, so a perfectly calibrated sensor can still be feeding an invalid model.
"Reproducing" an analysis re-runs it on the original data while "replicating" a study repeats it with newly collected data, so a finding can be reproducible and still fail to replicate.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Weathering" breaks rock down where it stands while "erosion" carries the loosened material away, so a sandstone facade can be deeply weathered without a grain of it having been eroded from the site.**

Weathering is disintegration in place, driven by frost, salt crystallisation, acid rain and biological action, and it leaves the debris where it forms. Erosion requires transport, by water, wind, ice or gravity, and it removes the products of weathering to somewhere else. On a sheltered stone facade the chemistry proceeds while nothing is carried off, which is why conservators find crumbling surfaces with the powder still sitting on them.

Breakdown and removal are separate processes that often occur together, and the facade example holds one without the other, so the distinction is drawn correctly.

**B) A retailer's "markup" is calculated on what the goods cost while its "margin" is calculated on what they sell for, so the same twenty pounds of difference represents a larger markup than margin.**

Markup expresses the difference between cost and price as a percentage of cost, so it answers how much has been added to what the buyer paid the supplier. Margin expresses the same difference as a percentage of the selling price, which is the figure that appears in accounts and comparisons between firms. Because the selling price is the larger denominator, the same cash difference always produces the smaller percentage when reported as margin.

Different denominators produce different percentages from identical cash, so the ranking the sentence gives follows arithmetically and the description is sound.

**C) A "projection" states what follows if a stated scenario holds while a "prediction" asserts what will actually happen, so a modelling group can publish several projections without contradicting itself.**

A projection is conditional by construction: given these assumptions about emissions, migration or fertility, the model produces this path. A prediction drops the condition and commits to an outcome, which is why forecasting agencies are careful about which word appears in a headline. Publishing a family of scenarios is a way of showing how sensitive the result is to assumptions rather than a display of indecision.

Conditional output and unconditional claim are different products, so a set of divergent projections is internally consistent in exactly the way the sentence describes.

**D) "Calibrating" an instrument adjusts its readings against a known standard while "validating" a model asks whether its outputs match independent observations, so a perfectly calibrated sensor can still be feeding an invalid model.**

Calibration is a comparison against a reference with a traceable value, and it corrects the instrument rather than the reasoning built on top of it. Validation tests whether a representation of the world behaves like the world, using data that were not used to build it. Good inputs into a poorly specified model produce confident nonsense, which is why environmental agencies require both steps.

The instrument and the model are checked against different references, so the failure mode the sentence describes is a real and familiar one rather than a contradiction in terms.

**E) "Reproducing" an analysis re-runs it on the original data while "replicating" a study repeats it with newly collected data, so a finding can be reproducible and still fail to replicate.**

Reproducibility tests the computational trail: given the same dataset and code, does the same table come out. Replication tests the finding itself: does a fresh sample, gathered independently, produce the same effect. A result can pass the first because the arithmetic is sound and fail the second because the original sample was unusual or the effect was a chance one.

**Tip:** Same data and same code is reproduction; new data and the same question is replication.

The two checks interrogate different things, so the combination the sentence describes is common enough to be a standing concern in research methods.
tasks.solution_overview: Each pair here divides a process into two stages or measures the same quantity against two different bases, so identify the base or the step before judging the claim. Breaking down and carrying away, adjusting an instrument and testing a model, re-running code and gathering fresh data all describe adjacent but distinct operations. Where percentages are involved, the decisive question is what sits in the denominator, and where models are involved it is whether a condition has been attached to the output.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five statements about pairs that describe the same behaviour while passing opposite judgements on it. Decide whether each account of the connotation is accurate.
statements: "Notorious" and "renowned" both report wide fame, but only the first assumes the fame is for something discreditable, so a prison notorious for overcrowding is not being complimented.
"Childish" is the appreciative term, describing an adult's unspoilt sense of wonder, while "childlike" condemns behaviour as immature.
"Miserly" is the neutral word for careful spending while "frugal" is the insult, so calling a scholarship fund's administrator frugal is a complaint about meanness.
"Propaganda" is a neutral synonym for "publicity", so a health ministry would ordinarily describe its own vaccination campaign as propaganda.
"Stubborn" is the admiring word and "tenacious" the critical one, so a researcher who keeps working on an unfashionable question for twenty years is being praised as stubborn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Notorious" and "renowned" both report wide fame, but only the first assumes the fame is for something discreditable, so a prison notorious for overcrowding is not being complimented.**

Both adjectives measure how widely something is known, and neither says anything about scale on its own. Renowned attaches that fame to achievement and invites admiration, while notorious attaches it to a fault, a scandal or a danger, and the noun that follows almost always names the trouble. Overcrowding is a failing, so the adjective is doing evaluative work rather than merely reporting reputation.

The shared meaning is reach and the difference is verdict, and the sentence keeps that verdict attached to the right word, so the account is accurate.

**B) "Childish" is the appreciative term, describing an adult's unspoilt sense of wonder, while "childlike" condemns behaviour as immature.**

Childlike is the sympathetic form, reserved for qualities of childhood that adults are glad to keep: curiosity, delight, directness, trust. Childish is dismissive and marks behaviour as beneath the age of the person showing it, which is why it collocates with sulking, squabbling and refusing to cooperate.
